analysis.one_liner: Restores the Glass-Steagall wall separating regular banking from investment banking.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Rep. Marcy Kaptur with 15 Democratic cosponsors, sat in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing or vote until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rebuild the Glass-Steagall wall between banks that hold insured deposits and firms that underwrite and trade stocks and bonds, repealing key parts of the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act that tore the wall down. Banks would have two years to cut ties with securities affiliates, and securities-firm executives could no longer sit on bank boards. Introduced in April 2023, it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank depositors and taxpayers. If the bill passed, a securities-market collapse could not directly drain customers' checking and savings accounts or drag insured banks into bailouts, because insured deposits would again be legally separate from securities trading [S2, S3]. Ordinary savers would also face fewer conflict-of-interest situations where the firm selling them an investment is also holding their deposits or steering their bank's advice [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Bars insured banks from affiliating with brokers, dealers, investment advisers, and investment companies, re-establishing the 1933 Glass-Steagall separation between everyday banking and securities trading that the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act repealed in 1999.
Gives existing bank-securities affiliations two years to unwind (with limited, reported extensions), so the change would not happen overnight but would end the combined model.

Prohibits securities-firm officers, directors, and employees from simultaneously serving at insured depository institutions, reducing conflicts of interest where the people running a bank also work for firms selling securities.

Writes the Supreme Court's strict interpretation in Investment Company Institute v. Camp into law and forbids banking agencies and courts from reading the new limits more narrowly, so regulators could not quietly loosen the wall the way the 1999 law's loophole process allowed.

analysis.who_pays: Large universal banks — financial holding companies that combine insured deposits with brokerage, investment advising, and securities underwriting — would have to divest or spin off their securities businesses within two years, along with the shareholders of those companies [S3]. Customers who value getting banking and investment services under one roof could lose that convenience, and the forced restructuring of some of the country's biggest banks would carry real transition costs [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large universal banks and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The bill would force a two-year, forced separation of securities operations from the largest banks — a massive restructuring of institutions that have operated under the combined model for 25 years, whose costs would partly land on bank customers and could roil markets during the transition.

The bill targets the mixing of insured deposits with securities firms, but the 2008 crisis's largest failures were standalone investment banks and insurers; supporters of the status quo argue re-separation would not by itself prevent future crises, a debate economists never fully settled.

The bill goes beyond a simple reinstatement by flatly prohibiting federal banking agencies and any U.S. court from interpreting the new limits more narrowly than the 1971 ICI v. Camp ruling, removing regulatory flexibility that even supporters of strong separation might want in unusual circumstances.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — making sure federally insured deposits cannot be put at risk by securities trading, and that taxpayers cannot be dragooned into rescuing the combination — is real and addresses a structural risk created by the 1999 repeal. The costs are also real: unwinding 25 years of conglomeration at the largest banks in two years would be disruptive and expensive, and the bill's hard-coded legal interpretation sacrifices regulatory flexibility for certainty. On balance, the bill asks concentrated financial interests to bear the disruption in exchange for a safer system for depositors, which is why the banks most affected would fight it hardest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the Return to Prudent Banking Act of 2023 on April 19, 2023, joined by seven original cosponsors including Reps. Norton, Omar, Tlaib, Pocan, Pingree, Wild, and Watson Coleman.
The bill gathered 15 cosponsors in total, all of them Democrats, with no Republican support.
The same day it was introduced, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large universal banks and their shareholders are better off: the combined model of insured deposits plus securities trading stays intact, and no bank had to reorganize. Depositors and taxpayers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large universal banks and their shareholders

for.name: Rep. Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its predecessor versions to restore the Glass-Steagall separation between commercial and investment banking.

for.name: 15 Democratic cosponsors (including Reps. Norton, Omar, Tlaib, Pocan, Pingree, Wild, and Watson Coleman)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all 15 of them Democrats, but the bill never advanced beyond the referral.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Patrick McHenry)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the action history shows only the April 19, 2023 referral and nothing else for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Large banks and financial industry trade groups
against.what_they_did: The universal-banking industry has long opposed reinstating Glass-Steagall, which would force its members to divest securities businesses; the committee's inaction meant the banks never had to fight it on the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so the partisan split was never formally tested beyond sponsorship.

industries.industry: Universal banks and financial holding companies
industries.note: These banks combine insured deposits with securities underwriting, brokerage, and investment advice — the exact combination the bill bans, on a two-year wind-down clock. Their interest in keeping the model runs against the public's interest in keeping deposit insurance and potential bailouts away from securities risk.

industries.industry: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and investment companies
industries.note: The bill ends their ability to affiliate with insured banks and bars their executives from serving on bank boards, but standalone securities firms that never touch deposits could continue operating as before.
Banks that already keep deposit-taking separate from securities trading would compete against giants that could no longer mix the two, narrowing a structural advantage of the largest institutions.
